subject: Gross Anatomy
objectives: Classify bones by shape and developmental origin
Identify the major regions of the axial and appendicular skeleton in domestic animals
Distinguish between compact and cancellous bone structure
overview:
**Osteology** is the study of bones — their structure, development, and function. In domestic animals the skeleton serves as a rigid framework, protects vital organs, enables locomotion, produces blood cells (in red marrow), and stores minerals (calcium, phosphorus).

Total bone counts vary by species: horse ~205, cattle ~207, dog ~319 (including sesamoids), cat ~230.

keyTerms.definition: The shaft of a long bone; composed mainly of compact bone surrounding the medullary cavity.
The expanded end of a long bone, covered by articular cartilage; contains cancellous bone.
Cartilaginous disc between diaphysis and epiphysis; site of longitudinal growth until skeletal maturity.
Dense fibrous membrane covering the outer surface of bone (except articular surfaces); source of osteoprogenitor cells.
Central canal of the diaphysis containing bone marrow (red = hematopoietic; yellow = adipose in adults).
Structural unit of compact bone: concentric bony lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal carrying vessels and nerves.
Thin vascular membrane lining the medullary cavity and the trabeculae of cancellous bone.

content:
## Classification by Shape

| Type | Description | Examples |
|------|-------------|----------|
| Long | Length > width; shaft + 2 epiphyses | Femur, humerus, radius |
| Short | Similar length and width | Carpals, tarsals |
| Flat | Thin, plate-like | Scapula, skull bones |
| Irregular | Complex shape | Vertebrae, hip bones |
| Sesamoid | Embedded in tendons | Patella, distal sesamoids |
| Pneumatic | Contain air sinuses | Frontal bone (cattle/horse) |

## Axial vs Appendicular

**Axial skeleton:** skull, hyoid, vertebral column, ribs, sternum.

**Appendicular skeleton:** pectoral girdle + forelimb, pelvic girdle + hindlimb.

## Bone Development

- **Intramembranous ossification:** flat bones of the skull form directly from condensed mesenchyme (no cartilage model).
- **Endochondral ossification:** most bones replace a cartilage model. Growth plates (physes) allow lengthening until closure at skeletal maturity.

## Species Notes

- **Horse:** splint bones (Mc2/Mc4; Mt2/Mt4) are vestigial metacarpals/metatarsals. The proximal sesamoids and distal sesamoid (navicular bone) are clinically important.
- **Cattle:** os cordis (heart bone) — a sesamoid-like ossification in the interventricular septum; unique to ruminants.
- **Dog:** 5 metacarpals retained; dewclaw (digit I) varies by breed.
highYield:
- **PRC Anatomy A.1–A.2 (Osteology/Arthrology)** — expect 3–5 items per 100-item exam.
- Know the bone classification table by shape — short-answer and MCQ staple.
- **Os cordis** in cattle is a classic unique-feature question.
- **Splint bone** questions: equine Mc2/Mc4 splints — periostitis causes 'splints' (exostosis), a lameness cause.
- **Periosteum** contains osteoprogenitor cells critical for fracture healing — NSAIDs and corticosteroids impair this (links to Pharmacology).
- Physis closure timing: earlier in small breeds; delayed by hypothyroidism, premature castration. A pathology and physiology cross-link.
- Red marrow → yellow marrow conversion occurs during growth: starts in extremities, moves centrally. In severe anemia the conversion reverses.
mnemonics:
**Bone types — "Lions Sometimes Fight In Small Pens":**
> **L**ong · **S**hort · **F**lat · **I**rregular · **S**esamoid · **P**neumatic

**Axial vs Appendicular:**
> **Axial** = along the **A**xis (skull, spine, ribs, sternum)
> **App**endicular = **App**endages (limbs + girdles)

**Bone layers outside → in:**
> **P**eriosteum → **C**ompact bone → **C**ancellous bone → **E**ndosteum → **M**arrow
> *"Please Cook Carefully, Even Marrow"*

subject: Systemic Physiology
objectives: Describe the phases of the cardiac cycle and their hemodynamic significance
Explain the generation and conduction of cardiac action potentials
Calculate cardiac output and explain how preload, afterload, and contractility affect it
Identify clinically relevant species differences in cardiac physiology
overview:
The heart is a dual pump. The **right side** receives deoxygenated blood and drives it through the pulmonary circulation; the **left side** receives oxygenated blood and drives it through the systemic circulation.

Cardiac physiology is high-yield for both **Veterinary Physiology** (A.4 Cardiovascular) and **Veterinary Medicine** (arrhythmia, heart failure, shock) and underpins drug targets in **Pharmacology** (digitalis, antiarrhythmics, vasodilators).

keyTerms.definition: Volume of blood pumped per minute. CO = HR × SV. Normal dog CO ≈ 100 mL/kg/min.
Volume ejected per beat. Determined by preload, afterload, and contractility.
End-diastolic ventricular volume (EDV); determined mainly by venous return. High preload → stretched sarcomeres → stronger contraction (Frank-Starling).
Resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject blood; essentially arterial pressure. High afterload → reduced SV.
Intrinsic force of contraction independent of preload/afterload. Increased by sympathetic stimulation, digitalis; decreased by heart failure, beta-blockers.
Within physiological limits, increased EDV (preload) stretches myofibers → greater cross-bridge overlap → greater force and SV.
Primary cardiac pacemaker in the right atrial wall. Sets intrinsic rate (60–80 bpm in dogs at rest). Automaticity due to the 'funny current' (If: slow Na+/Ca2+ influx during phase 4).
Period post-depolarization when the myocardium cannot be re-excited. Prevents tetanic contraction (critical for pumping function).

content:
## The Cardiac Cycle

| Phase | Valves | Key event |
|-------|--------|-----------|
| 1. Isovolumetric contraction | All closed | Ventricular pressure rises |
| 2. Rapid ejection | AoV/PV open | Blood exits; pressure peaks (systolic BP) |
| 3. Reduced ejection | AoV/PV open | Flow slows |
| 4. Isovolumetric relaxation | All closed | Ventricular pressure falls |
| 5. Rapid filling | AV valves open | ~80% of ventricular fill (passive) |
| 6. Atrial systole | AV valves open | ~20% fill; contributes more in tachycardia |

## Ventricular Action Potential

| Phase | Ion movement | Clinical relevance |
|-------|-------------|--------------------|
| 0 – Rapid depolarization | Na+ influx (fast channels) | Target of Class I antiarrhythmics |
| 1 – Early repolarization | K+ efflux, Cl- influx | — |
| 2 – Plateau | Ca2+ influx ≈ K+ efflux | Ca2+ triggers contraction; target of Ca2+-channel blockers |
| 3 – Repolarization | K+ efflux dominant | Target of Class III antiarrhythmics |
| 4 – Resting | Na+/K+ ATPase restores gradient | — |

## Species Resting Heart Rates

| Species | HR (bpm) |
|---------|----------|
| Horse | 28–44 |
| Cow | 48–84 |
| Sheep/Goat | 70–90 |
| Dog | 60–160 |
| Cat | 120–240 |
| Pig | 70–120 |

*(Higher HR in smaller species reflects higher mass-specific metabolic rate.)*

## Autonomic Control

- **Sympathetic (NE/E):** ↑ HR (chronotropy), ↑ contractility (inotropy), ↑ conduction velocity.
- **Parasympathetic (ACh/vagus):** ↓ HR, ↓ conduction through AV node (→ vagal bradycardia in horses).
- **Bainbridge reflex:** ↑ venous return → ↑ HR (stretch of RA → reflex tachycardia).
highYield:
- **CO = HR × SV** — know how each component affects CO clinically (tachycardia, hypovolemia, heart failure).
- **Frank-Starling** compensates in early heart failure (↑ EDV → maintains SV); decompensation = SV falls despite high preload.
- **Digitalis (digoxin):** inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na+ → less Ca2+ extrusion via Na+/Ca2+ exchanger → more intracellular Ca2+ → ↑ contractility. Also vagally mediated ↓ HR. Narrow therapeutic index; renal clearance — dose-adjust in renal failure.
- **Horses** have large SV (up to 3 L/beat at peak exercise); CO can reach 300 L/min in racing thoroughbreds. Resting sinus arrhythmia and second-degree AV block are normal in horses (high vagal tone).
- **Cats:** tachycardia (normal HR up to 240); hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the most common feline heart disease — impairs diastolic filling (diastolic dysfunction).
- **PRC Physiology A.4** (Cardiovascular) covers cardiac cycle, CO regulation, and BP control.
mnemonics:
**Cardiac cycle sequence — "I Run Every Interval, Running Atop":**
> **I**sovolumetric contraction → **R**apid ejection → **E**jection reduced → **I**sovolumetric relaxation → **R**apid filling → **A**trial systole

**Frank-Starling in one line:**
> *"The more you fill, the more you spill"* — greater stretch → greater output.

**Digitalis mechanism:**
> Block **Na/K pump** → ↑ Na inside → ↓ Na gradient → ↓ Na/Ca exchanger activity → **Ca stays in** → stronger beat.
> *"Block the pump, trap the calcium, squeeze the heart."*

subject: Entomology and Protozoology
objectives: Describe the life cycle of Toxoplasma gondii and identify definitive and intermediate hosts
Explain the routes of transmission relevant to veterinary and public health
Recognize clinical presentations in cats, small ruminants, and immunocompromised humans
Apply control and prevention strategies for toxoplasmosis
overview:
***Toxoplasma gondii*** is an obligate intracellular protozoan (Phylum Apicomplexa) with worldwide distribution. It is one of the most prevalent parasitic infections in humans and animals, with up to 30% seroprevalence in some human populations.

It is a **zoonotic** pathogen of major public health significance — capable of causing severe congenital disease and fatal encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts. Cats are the **only definitive host**; virtually any warm-blooded vertebrate can serve as an **intermediate host**.

keyTerms.definition: The host in which the sexual (gametogonic) phase of the parasite life cycle occurs. For T. gondii, this is exclusively felids (domestic cat and wild cats).
Host in which only asexual reproduction (schizogony/bradyzoite formation) occurs. For T. gondii: any warm-blooded vertebrate including humans, sheep, pigs, and rodents.
Environmentally resistant stage shed in cat feces. Sporulates to become infective within 1–5 days. Survives months to years in moist soil.
Rapidly dividing asexual form during acute infection. Disseminates via the blood/lymphatics; responsible for acute tissue destruction.
Slow-replicating form contained within tissue cysts (in muscle and brain). Associated with chronic/latent infection. Reactivates with immunosuppression.
Cyst containing thousands of bradyzoites, found in muscle, brain, and other organs of intermediate hosts. Infectious if ingested by a susceptible host.

Transplacental transmission of tachyzoites from a primarily infected mother. Causes abortion, stillbirth, or neonatal disease (hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis, encephalitis) in humans and small ruminants.

content:
## Life Cycle Summary

T. gondii has a **heteroxenous** (two-host) life cycle with three infectious stages:

| Stage | Found in | Infective to |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| Oocyst (sporulated) | Soil/environment | All hosts |
| Tachyzoite | Acute infection (any host) | Transmitted across placenta |
| Bradyzoite (tissue cyst) | Chronic infection (intermediate hosts) | Cat, other carnivores, humans |

## Routes of Transmission to Humans

1. **Ingestion of oocysts** — from contaminated soil, water, raw vegetables, cat litter boxes.
2. **Ingestion of tissue cysts** — undercooked meat (lamb, pork, venison); butcher workers at risk.
3. **Congenital** — primary maternal infection during pregnancy → transplacental tachyzoite transfer.
4. **Organ transplant / blood transfusion** — rare; important in immunosuppressed recipients.

## Clinical Disease

**Cats:** Primary infection usually subclinical; shed oocysts for only ~2 weeks. Clinical disease rare (fever, dyspnea, icterus — multisystemic); more severe with concurrent FIV/FeLV.

**Small ruminants (sheep, goats):** **Abortion** is the hallmark. Primary infection in early pregnancy → embryonic death and resorption. Late pregnancy → stillbirth or weak lambs with cotyledonary placentitis. Economic importance in sheep flocks.

**Humans:** Immunocompetent — usually asymptomatic or mild lymphadenopathy. Immunosuppressed (HIV/AIDS, organ transplant) → **cerebral toxoplasmosis** (ring-enhancing lesions on CT/MRI); potentially fatal. Congenital — classic triad: hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis.

## Diagnosis

- **Serology** (IgG/IgM ELISA, Sabin-Feldman dye test) — standard for humans and animals.
- **PCR** on amniotic fluid, CSF, or tissue.
- **Histopathology** — tachyzoites or cysts in tissue sections.
- Cats: fecal flotation for oocysts (unreliable — shed only 2 weeks; oocysts resemble Hammondia, Besnoitia).

## Treatment and Control

- **Treatment:** Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine (+ folinic acid to prevent bone marrow suppression) — humans. Clindamycin used in cats and dogs.
- **Prevention:** Thorough cooking of meat (>67°C); hand hygiene after gardening or handling cat litter; pregnant women/immunosuppressed: avoid cleaning cat litter; cover sandboxes.
highYield:
- **Only cats** (felids) are the definitive host — shed oocysts. This is the single most-tested T. gondii fact.
- **Sheep abortion** = classic VMLE scenario for T. gondii in intermediate hosts.
- Oocysts need **1–5 days to sporulate** in the environment before becoming infective (not immediately infectious when shed).
- **Congenital toxoplasmosis** risk: only if **primary infection** occurs during pregnancy (re-infection with latent bradyzoites does not cause congenital disease in most cases — important for counseling pregnant cat owners).
- **Immunosuppression** reactivates bradyzoites → tachyzoites → cerebral toxoplasmosis.
- Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine inhibit **folate synthesis** at two sequential steps (pyrimethamine inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; sulfadiazine inhibits dihydropteroate synthase) — cross-links to Pharmacology antimicrobial mechanism of action.
- **PRC Parasitology B** (Protozoology) covers T. gondii.
mnemonics:
**Hosts mnemonic:**
> *"Cats are the Final (definitive) Ones"* — only felids complete the sexual cycle.

**Three infectious stages — "OTB":**
> **O**ocyst (environment) · **T**achyzoite (acute) · **B**radyzoite (chronic/tissue cyst)

**Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine mechanism:**
> *"STOP Folate at Two Steps"*
> Sulfa → blocks dihydropteroate synthase (step 1)
> Pyrimethamine → blocks dihydrofolate reductase (step 2)

**Congenital risk rule:**
> *"First time is the worst time"* — only primary infection crosses the placenta.
